summary: This benchmark investigates the fault tolerance of write-gating mechanisms on a 32,768-voxel grid under isolated versus consecutive false pulse signals. The empirical results demonstrate that while multi-tick confirmation gates completely filter out isolated noise pulses, they remain vulnerable when false pulses mirror the valid multi-step confirmation pattern. The methodology is well controlled and statistically grounded with bootstrap confidence intervals, although evaluated on a stylized synthetic memory task.
strengths: Controlled ablation isolating pulse timing (separated vs. consecutive) while holding total pulse counts, transport commands, and world topologies identical.
Rigorous statistical reporting, including exact word counts, paired 95% bootstrap confidence intervals, and clear resampling units across 24 independent worlds.
Precise specification of experimental parameters, including voxel dimensions (32^3 = 32,768), transition counts, bit widths, and runtime resource footprints.
weaknesses: The evaluation is restricted to a synthetic voxel-grid memory environment rather than established deep learning sequential memory or external memory benchmarks.
Because no supporting repository was formally linked via the submission system, verification depends on external GitHub permalinks, warranting a text_only badge.
The qualitative finding—that pattern-matching gates fail when noise replicates their exact confirmation signature—is fundamentally intuitive and unsurprising from a formal automata perspective.
suggestions: Extend the benchmark to continuous or stochastic noise distributions beyond discrete single-tick and two-tick binary injection.
Evaluate whether learned adaptive temporal gating (such as chrono-initialized LSTMs or gated linear units) can infer pulse periodicity and separate true writes from synchronized bursts.

claims.text: A 32-side cubic grid consists of 32,768 voxels.
The setup connects to gated memory cells and work on matching gates to the time scales of sequences by Gers, Schmidhuber and Cummins (doi: 10.1162/089976600300015015).
Tallec and Ollivier (arXiv:1804.11188) analyzed gating mechanisms and time scales in recurrent networks.
Requiring confirmation improved exact recovery on separated pulses by 70.25 percentage points (100% vs. 29.75%).

novelty_vs_existing.title: Can recurrent neural networks warp time?
novelty_vs_existing.contribution: Applies temporal gating and time-scale separation concepts specifically to write-confirmation failure modes in a spatial 3D voxel reference architecture under synthetic pulse noise.
